notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.
Where a narrative continues one from the previous edition it says what has changed since; every edition is kept, so the reader can step back to where we were.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, since 2020, since 2008, since 1989 and since 1945, each the start of a regime the headlines are living inside, and sometimes a fifth that reaches further back and names its own starting year. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.

Each narrative sets one or two things to watch for: what should follow, by when, if its join is right. Later editions check them against their headlines; the ledger is data/watch.json and the count stands beside the narrative's firmness.

Each narrative looks ahead: the precedent its join most resembles, two or three paths with one favoured, and where the trajectory points over a decade. That is the writer's anticipation, drawn on what it knows of history and not only on the headlines; the expectations are the earliest dated signs of the favoured path, and are how the site checks it.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: After this week's Microsoft and air traffic failures, the fallback for shared digital systems is left to households and staff.

watch.what: A second European central bank or government advises households to keep cash or another offline means of payment for outages.
watch.because: If the reserve for shared systems is being placed on users, the week's failures should prompt more advice to households rather than new duties on the providers.

watch.what: Microsoft's post-incident report attributes the 12 November outage to a single change, component or region.
watch.because: The join holds that these services run through one system with no working fallback, so the cause should be one point of failure rather than several faults coinciding.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the CrowdStrike update of 19 July 2024, which stopped about 8.5 million Windows computers, grounded airlines and closed hospital systems for a day. It led to a US congressional hearing, a lawsuit by Delta and changes to how Microsoft lets security software reach the core of Windows, but no government required public services to keep a second system. The difference now is that central banks are advising households directly, as Spain and Portugal began to after the April 2025 blackout, and that the failures reach physical plant such as a swimming pool.

paths.name: Advice to households, not rules
paths.text: Over the next three months more authorities publish preparedness advice telling households to keep cash, water and paper copies, as Sweden, the Netherlands and now Portugal have done, while providers publish incident reports and promise fixes. No legal duty for public bodies to run a fallback outside their main cloud provider is adopted before mid-2027. This is favoured because advice is cheap and within a central bank's powers, while a duty needs legislation and money.
paths.sign: A central bank or civil protection agency publishes a recommended amount of cash for each household to keep.

paths.name: Regulators order public fallbacks
paths.text: A European government or the EU extends rules like the Digital Operational Resilience Act from banks to public administration, requiring email and records to keep a working copy outside one provider. This would most likely come through a review of public procurement in early 2027. It is less likely because cloud contracts are already signed and a second system costs more.
paths.sign: A government orders its ministries to keep a second email or records system that does not depend on Microsoft.

paths.name: Cash acceptance written into law
paths.text: Portugal or another euro area state passes a law obliging shops to accept cash and banks to keep cash machines running during outages, citing this week. The EU's regulation on cash as legal tender is still pending, and national laws passed within a year on the strength of one week are rare.
paths.sign: A parliament debates a bill requiring shops to accept cash, citing the November outages.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the number of providers that public services depend on is likely to shrink further as AI work concentrates in a few clouds. Unless law assigns the reserve to the providers, it stays with the citizen as cash at home and time spent waiting.

readings.change: Yesterday's narrative showed public services stopping when one system failed. Today the services are back and the reporting has turned to who keeps the backup: the Bank of Portugal advises households to hold cash, Microsoft promises a post-incident report, and US flights are still being cancelled by the thousand after the FAA lifted its ground stop.
readings.claim: A Microsoft outage that a Russian paper links to chlorine poisoning at a German swimming pool, a nationwide US ground stop blamed on overloaded old equipment, and Bank of Portugal advice to keep cash at home in case cash machines and MB Way fail together all reached the news on the same Saturday. Each concerns a shared system that many people depend on and that had no working fallback of its own. In each case the reserve that remained was held by the user: the passenger who waits, the staff on site, the household with notes in a drawer. The organisations that run the systems apologise and restore them, and none of these headlines reports one taking on a duty to keep a second system.

events.label: Microsoft outage linked to German pool poisoning
Microsoft apologises and restores Outlook and Teams
FAA ground stop blamed on old equipment
US flight cancellations continue on Saturday
Bank of Portugal advises cash at home
Nigerian banks push cashless payments

fragments.label: The Microsoft outage
fragments.text: Kommersant in Russia reports that a Microsoft outage led to chlorine poisoning at a swimming pool in Germany. In South Korea, Digital Daily reports that Microsoft officially apologised for Outlook and Teams going down, promising gradual recovery and a post-incident report, and Portugal's SAPO reports services back to normal. In Britain, International Business Times quotes users blaming the failure on a company that thinks AI can do the job better than people.

fragments.label: US air traffic
fragments.text: Ideastream in Cleveland reports that old technology was blamed for the ground stop, quoting that 'it got overloaded'. Portugal's Observador reports the FAA lifting the suspension at all US airports, but SudOuest in France, bdnews24 in Bangladesh, Tribuna do Norte in Brazil and LV12 in Argentina report thousands more flights cancelled or delayed on Saturday. Brazil's Diário do Grande ABC reports stranded passengers given a show by Simple Plan and Hoobastank, and ANSA carries Stephen King joking that aliens caused the chaos.

fragments.label: Cash in the drawer
fragments.text: SAPO reports the Bank of Portugal's recommendation on what to keep at home in case cash machines and MB Way fail at the same time. The question is framed as what the household should hold, not what the banks or the payment network must keep running. In Nigeria, Leadership reports banks and fintech firms deepening their cooperation on cashless transactions, the direction Portugal has already travelled.

fragments.label: The user holds the spare
fragments.text: What joins these is not one cause but one arrangement: a service many people depend on runs through a single system, and when it stops, the reserve is whatever the user has kept. The pool depended on a cloud service, the passengers on one federal flow-control system, Portuguese card payments on one interbank network. The Bank of Portugal's advice makes the arrangement explicit by asking households to plan for the failure of systems they do not control.

fragments.label: An apology, not an obligation
fragments.text: Microsoft's response as Digital Daily reports it is an apology and a report; the FAA's, as Observador reports it, is to lift the stop and let airlines recover. None of these headlines mentions compensation, a regulator's order or a second system. Nigeria's push to cashless payment shows the same dependence being built where it is not yet complete.

fragments.label: Three different failures
fragments.text: The failures do not share a cause. Microsoft's was a fault in a concentrated cloud service; the FAA's, by Ideastream's account, came from old equipment that could not carry its load, which is close to the opposite of cloud concentration. The Bank of Portugal's advice probably follows the Iberian blackout of April 2025 and may be standing guidance rather than a reaction to this week. The pool story reaches this collection only through a Russian paper, and a dosing failure may owe more to the pool's operator than to Microsoft.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The pandemic moved office work onto a few cloud services at once. Microsoft Teams went from about 20 million daily users in late 2019 to 75 million by April 2020, and email, schedules and building controls followed onto the same platforms. Cash use fell in the same years: the European Central Bank's surveys show cash's share of shop payments in the euro area falling from 79% in 2016 to 52% in 2024. Two failures then showed what that meant. On 19 July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike update stopped about 8.5 million Windows computers and Delta alone cancelled some 7,000 flights. On 28 April 2025 a blackout cut power across Spain and Portugal for most of a day, card terminals stopped and cash machines went dark. The Bank of Portugal advice reported by SAPO belongs to that sequence. The EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act, in force since January 2025, obliges banks to plan for outages, but it says nothing to the household, which this week is asked to plan for itself.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After 2008 the cheapest place to run anything became someone else's data centre. Amazon Web Services had opened in 2006; Microsoft's Azure followed in 2010 and Office 365 in 2011, and public bodies under spending cuts moved onto them because renting cost less than owning. Air traffic control went the other way. The FAA's NextGen modernisation, begun in 2007, has run for nearly two decades, and much of what it was meant to replace is still in service. On 11 January 2023 a damaged file in the decades-old NOTAM system halted every departure in the United States for the first time since September 2001. The ground stop that Ideastream reports was blamed on old technology that 'got overloaded' repeats that pattern. David Edgerton argues that the history of technology that matters is use and maintenance, not invention. The new cloud and the old flow-control computer have one trait in common: no one on site can run the service when the central system stops.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The open internet of the 1990s was designed to route around failure: packet switching sent traffic along any surviving path. What was built on top of it after Netscape's listing in August 1995 was a market, and markets reward scale, so many routes came to serve a few providers. Payments followed. Portugal's interbank operator SIBS built Multibanco from 1985 into one of Europe's most used cash machine networks, and MB Way, launched in 2015, put it on the phone; both run through one operator, which is why the Bank of Portugal can name them together. The last time governments organised a shared fallback at scale was the Year 2000 problem, when banks, airlines and utilities spent hundreds of billions of dollars checking code and printing paper procedures. Ulrich Beck described societies that produce risks they cannot insure and then argue over who carries them. In 1999 that cost was placed on institutions; the advice of this week places it on the account holder.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The order built after 1945 treated some services as public duties with a public reserve behind them. Central banks issued notes that anyone could hold without an account, and kept that duty as private card networks grew. In aviation, the collision of two airliners over the Grand Canyon in 1956 led Congress to create the Federal Aviation Agency in 1958 and put civil air traffic under one federal controller with radar and procedures the state owned and staffed. The research money that followed Sputnik in 1957 later built the networks these services now rent from private firms. For most of the period the reserve was institutional: paper strips in the control tower, cash in the bank vault, a manual for the pool attendant. This week's headlines, from a German pool to American departure boards, show services that still carry public duties but whose last reserve is the citizen's own cash and patience.

readings.line: Five years after Russia's 2021 draft treaties, NATO's shape is bargained in talks Europe does not lead.

watch.what: A European head of government or the EU says Europe's security or NATO membership cannot be settled at the 19 November meeting without Europeans.
watch.because: If NATO's terms are being raised in a format Europe does not lead, European governments should object to the format itself and not only to Russia's demands.

watch.what: Reports from the 19 November Putin-Xi-Trump meeting say nuclear weapons in Europe, NATO enlargement or Ukraine's membership were discussed.
watch.because: The join holds that Moscow's 2021 subjects have moved into this three-way format, so they should appear on its agenda and not only in Russian statements.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is Reykjavik in October 1986, where Reagan and Gorbachev discussed abolishing all ballistic missiles without consulting the European governments whose security rested on them, and Thatcher flew to Camp David weeks later to secure Britain's Trident. The talks led to the INF Treaty of 1987, which removed a whole class of missiles from Europe by a bilateral deal. The difference now is that a war is being fought in Europe, that China is the third party at the table, and that the American president has questioned the alliance itself.

paths.name: Europe objects, nothing is signed
paths.text: The 19 November meeting produces statements on arms control and on further Ukraine talks, European governments object to being absent, and no NATO decision on Ukraine is taken before the alliance's next summit in 2027. Accession needs every member's ratification, and Poland, the Baltic states and others would not trade territory for it. This is favoured because every party gains from talking and none can deliver NATO membership alone.
paths.sign: European leaders issue a joint statement after 19 November insisting on their part in any settlement.

paths.name: Guarantees traded for Donbas
paths.text: By spring 2027 Washington and Moscow agree a framework in which Ukraine cedes or freezes the line in Donbas and receives security guarantees short of membership, with Britain and France asked to supply forces. Membership would be replaced by guarantees because membership needs unanimity. This follows the reported offer but depends on Kyiv accepting a loss of territory.
paths.sign: A draft document is reported that offers Ukraine security guarantees in exchange for terms on Donbas.

paths.name: Europe opens its own channel
paths.text: European governments, as Tusk's statement suggests they are discussing, open formal talks of their own with Russia before the end of the year. This is unlikely because the EU has no agreed view on who would speak for it and several members refuse contact with Moscow.
paths.sign: A European envoy is named to hold direct talks with Russia on behalf of several EU states.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the trajectory points to European states building more of their own defence and nuclear arrangements, French and British, in pairs and small groups, while the terms of Europe's security are discussed in Washington, Moscow and Beijing.

readings.claim: Volodymyr Zelensky says Washington floated Ukraine giving up Donbas in return for NATO membership; the Kremlin announces that Putin, Xi and Trump will meet on 19 November; Russian officials demand that Britain give up its nuclear cover for Europe and say Europe would be safer without NATO; and Donald Tusk speaks about which European countries will take part in talks with Russia. These are the subjects of the draft treaties Moscow published in December 2021: who may join NATO and which weapons protect Europe. They are now raised in a format led by the United States, Russia and China, while European governments argue about whether they have a seat. Meanwhile Europe's own defence projects are settled pair by pair, with Italy reported to have kept Germany out of its fighter programme.

events.label: US floats Donbas for NATO membership
Putin, Xi and Trump to meet
Russia demands end to Europe's nuclear cover
Tusk on who joins talks with Russia
ANSA traces Helsinki to Moscow's 2021 draft
Italy's bilateral defence deals exclude Germany

rungs.label: What is now on the table

fragments.label: Territory for membership
fragments.text: bdnews24 in Bangladesh, DW's Hausa service and China's NBD all carry Zelensky's account that the United States suggested Ukraine cede territory, named by bdnews24 as Donbas, in exchange for joining NATO. None of the three reports the idea from an American source.

fragments.label: A meeting of three
fragments.text: Anadolu reports the Kremlin's statement that Putin, Xi and Trump will hold a trilateral meeting on 19 November, and Handelsblatt places it on the sidelines of a summit in China. Lebanon's Al-Anbaa asks whether the three will hold nuclear talks.

fragments.label: Moscow's demands
fragments.text: Unian, citing the Telegraph, reports that Russia demands Britain give up its nuclear shield for Europe, and ENIKOS in Greece reports a Russian statement that Europe would be safer without NATO. Japan's 47NEWS reports that Russia has not changed its hard line in the Ukraine talks. ANSA runs a piece tracing a line from the Helsinki Final Act of 1975 to the draft Moscow treaty of 2021.

fragments.label: European arrangements
fragments.text: Unian reports Tusk's statement on which countries will take part as Europe prepares for talks with Russia, a question about attendance rather than terms. Kommersant, citing the Financial Times, reports that Italy did not allow Germany into joint fighter development, and iefimerida reports that Greece's parliament has received an agreement with Italy on policing airspace against non-military threats.

rungs.label: The 2021 agenda in a new forum

fragments.label: Same subjects, different table
fragments.text: Moscow's December 2021 drafts asked for an end to NATO enlargement and for limits on Western forces and weapons in Europe. This week's headlines raise both: membership as something that can be traded, and British nuclear cover as something Europe should give up. What has changed is who discusses them: Washington leads, Beijing is invited, and Europe's question, by Tusk's account, is who attends.

fragments.label: Europe arranges itself in pairs
fragments.text: While the larger questions are raised elsewhere, Europe's own defence is being arranged in bilateral deals: Italy with Greece on airspace, Italy with partners other than Germany on fighters. These are the choices of states hedging inside an alliance whose terms others are discussing.

fragments.label: Talk is not a deal
fragments.text: The American idea is known only from Zelensky's account, and NATO accession needs ratification by all 32 members, so no one in Washington can trade membership alone. Russia has demanded limits on British and French nuclear forces in various forms for years. The three-way meeting may be about arms control and trade between the largest nuclear powers rather than about Europe, and Italy's fighter decision is an industrial quarrel over work shares. What these events do not share is an author: one is a reported American idea, one a Russian talking point, one an Italian procurement choice.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: Russia's full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 followed two draft treaties Moscow published in December 2021, asking NATO to stop enlarging and to pull forces back to where they stood in 1997. NATO refused, and the war then produced the opposite of what the drafts asked: Finland joined in April 2023 and Sweden in March 2024. Russia moved tactical nuclear weapons into Belarus in 2023, and in March 2025 President Macron offered to discuss extending French nuclear deterrence to European partners. New START, the last limit on American and Russian strategic forces, was due to expire in February 2026. By these headlines, talks to end the war are now led by Washington, with Zelensky reporting an American idea of Donbas for membership, a Russian demand that Britain give up its nuclear cover for Europe, and a three-way meeting with Beijing on 19 November. Each is a subject Moscow put in writing in 2021, and the European governments that would carry the result are still discussing, as Tusk's statement shows, who among them will attend.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: At its Bucharest summit in April 2008 NATO declared that Ukraine and Georgia 'will become members' without giving either a plan to get there, and Russia went to war in Georgia four months later. After Crimea in 2014 the talks that followed, which produced the Minsk agreements of 2014 and 2015, were run in the Normandy format by France and Germany with Russia and Ukraine, and Washington stayed outside. That arrangement is now reversed: the United States leads and European capitals ask for places. Britain's position changed most. After the 2016 referendum it left the European Union's foreign policy machinery but kept its nuclear force assigned to NATO, which is why the Russian demand reported by Unian is addressed to London rather than Brussels. The same years split Europe's defence industry into rival groups: Italy, Britain and Japan merged their fighter plans in 2022 while France, Germany and Spain pursued another, and Kommersant now reports Rome keeping Berlin out.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The settlement after the Cold War rested on documents that this week's headlines reopen. The INF Treaty had removed intermediate-range missiles from Europe by 1991. The Budapest Memorandum of December 1994 gave Ukraine assurances from the United States, Britain and Russia in exchange for giving up the nuclear weapons left on its soil. The NATO-Russia Founding Act of May 1997 accompanied enlargement to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic in 1999 and to the Baltic states and others in 2004. Russia's case since Putin's Munich speech of February 2007 has been that enlargement broke promises made in 1990; NATO's has been that each state chooses its alliance. Ivan Krastev and Stephen Holmes describe these years as ones in which Central Europe imitated the West in order to join it. The idea reported this week, membership offered in exchange for territory, treats the alliance as something to be traded, which neither side of the 1990s argument accepted.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: NATO was founded in April 1949 on one promise, Article 5, with American nuclear weapons behind it. Britain tested its own bomb in 1952 and France in 1960, so two European states kept forces they could use without Washington's consent. In practice the superpowers often decided Europe's security without Europeans: at Reykjavik in 1986 Reagan and Gorbachev came close to abolishing ballistic missiles without consulting the allies who hosted them. The Helsinki Final Act of 1975, which ANSA traces forward to Moscow's 2021 draft, was the exception, signed by 35 states including every European country, accepting both fixed borders and each state's right to choose its alliances. Tony Judt describes a western Europe rebuilt under someone else's guarantee. A meeting of the American, Russian and Chinese leaders on 19 November, if Europe's alliance and nuclear cover are among its subjects, is nearer to Yalta in February 1945 than to Helsinki.

readings.line: Five years into the price rise, incomes set by formula or grant have fallen furthest behind, and their holders now protest or close.

watch.what: The French government announces a rise in a pension, allowance or minimum income, or grants police a higher risk allowance.
watch.because: If the protests are attempts to reprice incomes set by rule, the first concessions should come as changes to those rules rather than as price controls.

watch.what: A European government brings forward or tops up next year's pension or benefit indexation, naming living costs.
watch.because: The join predicts that incomes fixed by formula, not wages in general, are where governments will be forced to act first.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the gilets jaunes, who began protesting on Saturday 17 November 2018 over a fuel tax. Within a month President Macron announced about 10 billion euros of measures, including a higher in-work benefit and the cancellation of a tax rise for most pensioners, and the protests shrank through 2019. The difference now is that France's debt is higher and its parliament has refused budgets, so a similar package is harder to pass, and the same gap is reported in Italy, Argentina and Canada at once.

paths.name: Top-ups for the loudest groups
paths.text: Before the end of the year France grants targeted increases, a higher risk allowance for police and a one-off payment or indexation change for low pensions, without rewriting the rules. Other governments follow with one-off payments in their 2027 budgets. This is favoured because one-off sums fit inside existing budgets, while new indexation rules commit every future one.
paths.sign: France's interior ministry announces a higher risk allowance for police officers.

paths.name: The protests become strikes
paths.text: French unions join the Saturday protests with a national strike in December or January, naming food and fuel prices, and the claim spreads to public-sector pay. This becomes likely if the budget is again refused and no concession is made.
paths.sign: The main French union confederations announce a joint national strike day over pay and prices.

paths.name: Formulas rewritten to follow prices
paths.text: A government changes a pension or pay formula so that it follows prices more closely, as Italy's scala mobile once did for wages. EU deficit rules and the cost to future budgets make this unlikely within a year.
paths.sign: A bill to index pensions or public pay to inflation more than once a year is introduced.

ahead.decade: Ageing populations mean that a larger share of income each year will be set by rule rather than by market. The gap between the two speeds of adjustment will be a main argument over public budgets in Europe and South America through the 2030s.

readings.claim: On the fifth Saturday of protests against the cost of living in France, demonstrators tell franceinfo they have little left after paying for everything, while French police demand a higher risk allowance. In Italy a simulation shows a contributory pension in 2028 worth over 13,000 euros a year less than one twenty years earlier, and a restaurant gives up its Michelin star because prices rose and salaries did not; in Argentina a former judge warns of delays in retirees' claims, and in Canada a disability non-profit closes after fourteen years because of rising costs. In each case the income in question is set by a law, a decree or a grant that changes far more slowly than prices. The people who live on those incomes are the ones protesting or closing, while incomes that reprice through markets do not appear in these headlines.

events.label: France's fifth Saturday of price protests
French police demand higher risk allowance
Italian pension simulation shows lost income
Restaurant gives up Michelin star over costs
Argentine retirees' claims delayed
Rising costs close a Canadian charity

fragments.label: Saturdays and police pay
fragments.text: franceinfo reports a fifth Saturday of protests against the high cost of living, with a demonstrator saying that once everything is paid little is left. ENIKOS in Greece reports clashes between protesters and police in Paris, and ANSA reports France's interior ministry counting 219 detained and ten officers slightly injured. franceinfo separately reports growing anger among police officers demanding an increase in their risk allowance, so the officers policing the protests have their own claim on a fixed payment.

fragments.label: Italy, Argentina, Canada
fragments.text: Il Messaggero runs a simulation showing contributory pensions in 2028 losing over 13,000 euros a year compared with twenty years earlier. Corriere della Sera reports a restaurant giving up its Michelin star, its owner saying prices have gone crazy and salaries have not. Cadena 3 in Argentina reports a former judge's strong warning over delays in retirees' claims in Buenos Aires, and CBC reports a disability non-profit closing after 14 years because of rising costs.

rungs.label: Incomes that wait for a rule

fragments.label: Set by formula
fragments.text: What these incomes share is how they are set. An Italian contributory pension follows a formula fixed in law; a French police risk allowance is fixed by decree; an Argentine pension is adjusted by formula and, when that falls short, by court claims that take years; a Canadian charity lives on grants agreed in advance. Prices for food, rent and fuel change every month, and these incomes change only when a law or a negotiation does.

fragments.label: Protest as a demand to revise
fragments.text: Read this way, the French Saturdays and the police claim are attempts to force a revision of a rule before its due date, and the Canadian closure and the restaurant's simpler menu are what happens where no one can protest. The restaurant owner's sentence about prices and salaries states the gap directly.

fragments.label: Different gaps, different causes
fragments.text: The Italian simulation compares pensions with those of twenty years ago and measures the design of the 1995 pension reform, not this year's prices. Argentina's pension claims have been delayed under many governments and many inflation rates. The French protests have their own political history, the police claim is about danger as much as cost, and the restaurant is making a business choice about what cooking it can afford. What these events do not share is a cause: one is a pension rule, one a pay claim, one a charity's budget, and the overlap may be no more than that rising prices touch everything.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: Euro area inflation reached 10.6% in October 2022, the highest since the euro began, and Canada's peaked at 8.1% in June 2022. Prices set in markets moved within months; incomes set by rule moved a year or more later, if at all. France raised its pension age from 62 to 64 in 2023 without a final vote, under Article 49.3. Italy cut the indexation of larger pensions in its 2023 budget. In Argentina inflation passed 200% in 2023, and in 2024 President Milei vetoed a law raising pensions, after which retirees protested outside Congress every Wednesday. Canadian charities on multi-year grants found the grants fixed while rents and salaries rose. By these headlines the war with Iran has since added a fuel shock to that gap. The people now protesting or closing, French demonstrators on a fifth Saturday, French police, Argentine pensioners and a Canadian disability charity, are those whose income waits for a law, a decree or a grant round.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The 2008 crisis made public debt the measure governments were judged by, and pensions and public pay were where they looked first. In December 2011 Italy's Monti government passed the Fornero law, raising the pension age and freezing indexation for pensions above three times the minimum. Greece cut pensions repeatedly under its bailout programmes from 2010. In Argentina a change to the pension formula in December 2017 brought riots outside Congress. In France the gilets jaunes began on Saturday 17 November 2018 over a fuel tax and turned into weekly protests about what remained at the end of the month, the complaint franceinfo's protesters repeat. Adam Tooze traces how the cost of the crisis was spread through budget rules rather than single decisions. Il Messaggero's simulation, a pension in 2028 worth over 13,000 euros a year less than one of twenty years earlier, measures that spreading for one Italian worker.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: In the 1990s the countries in this narrative rewrote how incomes are fixed. Italy's Dini reform of 1995 moved pensions from a share of final salary to an amount based on lifetime contributions, phased in so that its full effect falls on those retiring from the late 2020s; the 13,000 euros in Il Messaggero's simulation is that design reaching its first full generation. Argentina privatised its pension system in 1994 and took it back into the state in 2008, and its courts have carried a large backlog of claims over indexation ever since. In France the Juppé plan of November 1995 to reform public-sector pensions met weeks of strikes and was withdrawn, which taught French governments that pay and pension rules change only at the cost of the street. The euro, from 1999, removed devaluation as a way to adjust all wages at once. Albert Hirschman's terms fit: people who cannot leave a pay rule use voice.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The welfare states built after 1945 turned income in old age, sickness and dangerous work into rules rather than favours. France created its sécurité sociale by ordinances in October 1945. Britain followed the Beveridge report of 1942 with the National Insurance Act of 1946. Italy tied wages to prices through the scala mobile, strengthened in 1975, cut in 1984 and abolished in 1992. Argentina wrote the rights of the elderly into Perón's constitution of 1949. Karl Polanyi argued in 1944 that societies would pull back markets that set livelihoods without regard to people, and the post-war rules were that pulling back. Their weakness is timing: a rule revised once a year cannot follow prices that change every week. The French police officers asking for a higher risk allowance, an amount fixed by decree for a dangerous job, are asking for one piece of the post-war arrangement to be repriced.

readings.line: Five years of high food prices and cut supply routes have put governments back into selling food and choosing which crops are grown.

watch.what: A government in Europe, Asia or Africa announces fertiliser subsidies, emergency imports or export curbs and cites the Hormuz closure.
watch.because: If supply cuts are pulling states into food provision, the fertiliser shortage named in the Netherlands should bring a public purchase or subsidy before spring planting, not only a warning.

watch.what: Another city or national government outside Egypt and the United States announces publicly run or publicly subsidised food shops.
watch.because: The join holds that public authorities are taking back the selling of food, so New York's stores should not stay an isolated case.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the food price crisis of 2007 and 2008, when export bans by India, Vietnam and others nearly tripled rice prices and there were protests in more than thirty countries, including Senegal and Egypt. Governments launched self-sufficiency programmes and widened subsidised sales, and when prices fell in the 2009 recession many programmes were scaled back. The difference now is that the shock reaches fertiliser before food, through a closed strait, and that a rich American city is opening public shops for reasons of price rather than scarcity.

paths.name: Fertiliser aid before spring planting
paths.text: Through the winter, governments in Europe, South Asia and Africa buy or subsidise fertiliser and widen public food sales, and the measures are written into 2027 budgets. This is favoured because planting decisions for spring are made in the coming months and a shortage of inputs cannot be waited out the way a price spike can.
paths.sign: A government announces a fertiliser subsidy or state purchase and names the Hormuz blockade.

paths.name: Strait reopens, plans shrink
paths.text: If talks reopen Hormuz in the coming weeks, urea and ammonia prices fall, the warnings stop, and public schemes shrink to those already promised, such as New York's stores. This is possible because earlier editions reported oil output close to pre-war levels and talks continuing.
paths.sign: Urea or ammonia prices are reported falling after shipping resumes through Hormuz.

paths.name: Export bans on staples return
paths.text: Large rice or wheat exporters restrict sales abroad to protect their own supply, as in 2008 and 2022, and staple prices rise sharply. Rice stocks are larger now than in 2008, which makes this unlikely without a harvest failure.
paths.sign: India or Vietnam announces a ban or a new duty on rice exports.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the trajectory points to food being treated again as part of national security, with public stocks, domestic fertiliser plants and state retail, as in the 1970s, at the expense of the open trade the 1995 WTO agreement assumed.

readings.claim: In the Netherlands, Nieuws.nl reports that a fertiliser shortage caused by the Hormuz blockade threatens food security; in Yemen, Marib's farmers have abundant harvests and no open markets; in Senegal, officials call rice an essential pillar of food sovereignty; New York is spending $70 million on five city-run grocery stores; Egypt's prime minister inspects a permanent state food fair; and Fortune reports that when Walmart leaves a town, nearby shops lose sales rather than gaining them. Together they show public authorities taking back roles in food supply that markets and traders held for three decades: choosing what is grown, securing inputs and selling to the public. The supply cuts at one end of the list are the reasons given for the public roles at the other.

events.label: Fertiliser shortage from Hormuz blockade
Marib farmers cut off from markets
Walmart exits leave neighbouring shops worse off
New York funds city-run grocery stores
Egypt's prime minister tours state food fair
Senegal pushes rice for food sovereignty

fragments.label: Inputs, routes and shops
fragments.text: Nieuws.nl in the Netherlands reports that the fertiliser shortage caused by the Hormuz blockade threatens food security. Al Jazeera reports from Marib that farmers with abundant harvests pay the price of war because their outlets are closed. Fortune reports that when Walmart pulls out of a town, the stores next door do not pick up its shoppers and their sales are down 20% a year later.

rungs.label: Public bodies as grocer and planner

fragments.label: Selling and planning
fragments.text: Fortune reports New York City spending $70 million on five city-run grocery stores pricing essentials 30% below retail, with bodegas fighting back. Al-Watan reports Egypt's prime minister inspecting the permanent food goods exhibition in Mansoura. Le Soleil quotes the head of Mbour's rural development service calling rice an essential pillar of Senegal's food sovereignty, and reports farmers in Pointe-Sarène taking up the Nerica variety.

fragments.label: Who makes sure there is food
fragments.text: The question decided in each case is who makes sure that food is available at a price people can pay. Where inputs are cut, as with Gulf fertiliser, where routes are closed, as in Marib, or where a dominant retailer leaves, as in Fortune's study, the answer in these headlines is a public body: a city that sells groceries, a state that runs food fairs, a ministry that plans the national crop.

fragments.label: Who loses
fragments.text: New York's plan already has opponents in the bodegas, the small shops a city store would undercut. The same trade-off exists in Egypt and Senegal, where state outlets and national crop targets compete with private importers. Public supply protects the buyer and takes business from the trader.

fragments.label: Old policies and one new shock
fragments.text: Only the fertiliser story is new this week. Egypt has run subsidised food outlets since the 1940s, Senegal's rice plans date from the 2008 crisis, and New York's stores were an election promise made in 2025. Marib's problem is war, not policy, and food is always reported somewhere. What these events do not share is a cause: one is a blockade, one a mayor's programme, one a war and one a retailer's exit, and nothing in the headlines links the New York stores to the Gulf.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The pandemic disrupted food supply chains in 2020, and Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 pushed the FAO food price index to its record of about 160 in March 2022. Fertiliser followed gas: European ammonia plants cut output when gas prices rose that year, and urea prices more than doubled. The Gulf is a large exporter of urea and ammonia, with Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Oman among the leading sellers, so a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which Nieuws.nl now links to a fertiliser shortage, reaches the next harvest rather than the present one. In New York, Zohran Mamdani won the mayoral election of November 2025 promising city-owned grocery stores, and the $70 million for five stores reported by Fortune is that pledge being built. American food prices rose roughly a quarter between 2020 and 2024, and the stores are priced against that rise.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: In 2007 and 2008 world rice prices nearly tripled after India, Vietnam and others restricted exports, and there were food protests in more than thirty countries. Dakar had riots in March 2008, and in Egypt people died in bread queues that spring while the army was ordered to bake. The lesson governments drew was that a country importing its staple can be refused it. Senegal launched its Great Agricultural Offensive for Food and Abundance in 2008 and has set rice self-sufficiency targets since, which is the background to Le Soleil's interviews about rice and the Nerica variety in Pointe-Sarène. The protests of 2011 in Cairo began partly over bread prices, and Egypt's state outlets and permanent food fairs, like the one in Mansoura the prime minister visited, grew in the years after 2016 as devaluation raised import costs. The phrase food sovereignty moved in this period from farmers' movements into ministries.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The 1990s handed food to markets. The WTO's Agreement on Agriculture of 1995 limited subsidies and encouraged countries to buy staples where they were cheapest, and Senegal, like much of West Africa, came to rely on imported broken rice from Asia after the CFA franc was devalued in 1994 and state marketing boards were wound up. In rich countries retail concentrated: Walmart opened its first grocery supercentre in 1988 and became the largest food seller in the United States, so its arrival and departure decided whether many small towns had a full grocer. Fortune's report that neighbouring shops lose a fifth of their sales a year after Walmart leaves describes the end point: the large store displaced the small ones, so its exit leaves a gap no trader fills. James C. Scott warned against planners who cannot see what they count; these decades tested the opposite case, in which no one planned the supply at all.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: After 1945 feeding people was a state task. Britain kept rationing until 1954. Egypt's ration cards, introduced during the Second World War, became after 1952 a permanent system of subsidised bread, sugar and oil, and an attempt to cut bread subsidies in January 1977 brought riots that made the government reverse within two days. India's Green Revolution of the late 1960s rested on state-supplied fertiliser and guaranteed prices. Because the Haber-Bosch process, industrialised from 1913, made nitrogen fertiliser from gas, much of the world's food came to depend on it, which is why a shortage reported in the Netherlands is a food story. The United States chose federal food stamps from 1964 rather than public shops, and New York's city-run stores depart from that by selling food instead of paying for it. Marib's farmers, with harvests and no buyers, show the oldest problem of all: the food exists and the road to market does not.
